articles.title: Solar flares, geomagnetic storms & the brain
articles.summary: What solar flares and geomagnetic storms physically do, what has been measured about brain rhythms and Earth-strength fields, and where Dr. Jack Kruse's storm-day headache and intracranial pressure framework goes beyond the evidence.

sections.heading: Flares, CMEs, and storms are different events
sections.body: A solar flare is a burst of light from the Sun—mostly X-ray and extreme ultraviolet. It arrives in about 8 minutes, is absorbed high in the atmosphere on the sunlit side of Earth, and can black out shortwave radio there for minutes to hours. NOAA rates these blackouts R1 (minor, M1 flares) to R5 (extreme, X20). A coronal mass ejection (CME) is different: a cloud of magnetized plasma that sometimes launches with a large flare and takes roughly 1–3 days to reach Earth. If its field is oriented southward, it compresses the magnetosphere and drives a geomagnetic storm, measured by the Kp index and rated G1 (Kp 5) to G5 (Kp 9). Storms bring auroras, ULF waves, and induced currents in the ground and in power lines. Not every flare has a CME, and not every CME hits Earth.

sections.heading: What reaches you at ground level
sections.body: The atmosphere absorbs flare X-rays long before they reach the ground, so the direct flare effect is on the upper atmosphere, not on skin or eyes. Storm-time changes in the magnetic field at the surface are typically tens to a few hundred nanotesla—usually under 1% of the roughly 25,000–65,000 nT main field shown in the Place view—though they can change quickly, and they are larger at high latitudes. That is a small but real change in the field you live in, and it is the part of space weather most relevant to any biological effect.

sections.heading: What this app shows
sections.body: The home screen shows an alert when an X-class flare (R3 strong blackout or larger) has peaked in the last 24 hours. The Place view lists the largest flares of the past day and week, the number of M- and X-class flares this week, the current and 24-hour peak Kp, and whether your ZIP code was on the sunlit side when the latest flare peaked. Data come from NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center. A flare alert is a heads-up that a storm may follow in 1–3 days; the Kp value tells you whether one is actually under way.

sections.heading: Brain rhythms and Earth's field: what has been measured
sections.body: The brain's alpha rhythm (about 8–12 Hz) is generated largely by thalamocortical circuits. The Schumann resonance—electromagnetic standing waves in the cavity between Earth and the ionosphere—has its fundamental near 7.83 Hz. The overlap in frequency has been noted for decades; a causal coupling between the two has not been demonstrated. The strongest direct evidence that human brains register Earth-strength fields is Wang, Kirschvink and colleagues (eNeuro, 2019): in a shielded lab, rotating a field of geomagnetic strength produced drops in alpha-band power in some participants, with substantial differences between people. That study did not test solar storms, headaches, or health outcomes. Population studies have reported associations between geomagnetic activity and migraine, cardiovascular events, and hospital admissions, but results are mixed and effects are small.

sections.heading: Where Dr. Jack Kruse's teaching is specific
sections.body: In a recent forum post, Kruse describes a severe solar storm as a geomagnetic induction front rather than just a radio disturbance. In his account, the compressed magnetosphere drives telluric currents and ULF waves that phase-jam the Schumann resonance. The thalamus then loses its spatial reference frame: alpha pacing drops in amplitude and desynchronizes, structured water around neurons loses capacitance (he describes its dielectric constant falling from about 160 to 78), cerebrospinal fluid thickens, glymphatic drainage slows, and intracranial pressure rises. He presents this as the cause of storm-day headaches and circadian disruption in healthy people. For people with glioma, he argues the same storm pushes already damaged mitochondria into failure, producing edema, severe headaches, and seizures. He cites Petrov (2002), Cifra (2014), Wang (2019), Michaeli (2019), and Picard (2019), and he tied two large Panama earthquakes to the same storm.

sections.heading: What is solid, what is framework
sections.body: Solid: flares, CMEs, and geomagnetic storms; their effects on the ionosphere, radio, satellites, and power grids; and lab evidence that some human brains respond to changes in Earth-strength fields. Suggestive but mixed: population associations between storm days and headaches or cardiovascular events. Earthquakes: seismologists have repeatedly tested whether solar or geomagnetic activity triggers earthquakes and have not found a reliable link. articles.title: Solar noon sun for vitamin D
articles.summary: Why UVB on skin near solar noon is the natural vitamin D pathway, how it differs from morning eye light, and when sun comes before routine pills.

sections.heading: What this habit is
sections.body: Solar noon sun for vitamin D means short, non-burning outdoor skin exposure when the sun is high—arms, legs, or more when season and skin type allow. Morning outdoor light to the eyes trains circadian clocks (Sunrise). Vitamin D is a separate solar product: UVB on skin converts 7-dehydrocholesterol toward vitamin D₃, which liver and kidney further activate. Eyes do not make meaningful vitamin D; skin does.

sections.heading: Why solar noon matters
sections.body: When the sun is highest, more UVB reaches the ground than at low solar angles. Local solar noon on Place is the practical window for efficient D synthesis per minute, latitude and season permitting. Mid-morning and late afternoon often feel pleasant but deliver more UVA relative to UVB. That does not mean burn yourself at noon—it means prefer a short outdoor block near solar noon over random indoor time when UV season allows. High-latitude winters may not provide enough UVB for repletion.

sections.heading: What mainstream physiology says
sections.body: Dermatology and endocrinology agree: sensible sun helps vitamin D status; deficiency is common indoors and at high latitude. Oral vitamin D₃ raises blood 25(OH)D and is standard care when labs show deficiency, in deep winter, or when sun is impractical. Synthesis and supplements both work in clinical medicine. Responsible sun hygiene means non-burning exposure, gradual build, and respect for skin type, medications, and skin-cancer history—ask a clinician for labs and dermatology advice.

sections.heading: Practical solar noon habit
sections.body: Use the solar-noon time shown in Place context. When UV season allows, get outdoors with unprotected skin for a short interval—often roughly 10–20 minutes for lighter skin at mid-latitudes in summer, shorter in strong sun, longer for darker melanin. Build gradually. Window glass blocks UVB; indoor “sun” does not count. Practice Outside Time in the peak-sun slot (±1.5 hours around local solar noon), full sun when you can, with duration. Pair with the sunrise practice so the Light arc is eyes at dawn plus skin at noon.

sections.heading: When supplements still belong
sections.body: Winter at high latitude, night-shift life, malabsorption, osteoporosis plans, or confirmed low 25(OH)D are legitimate supplement contexts—follow your clinician. The lifestyle ordering here is: default to solar noon skin when UV exists; do not use a daily gummy to excuse zero outdoor UV all summer. Re-test labs if you change sun habits or doses. Seafood and fortified foods add dietary D but do not replace the UVB message for skin synthesis.

sections.heading: What is solid vs framework
sections.body: Solid ground: UVB on skin makes vitamin D; solar angle and latitude matter; supplements raise 25(OH)D when sun cannot. Framework / teaching layer: that chronic high-dose oral D without UV “short-circuits” natural production or that pills miss essential solar frequencies the capsule cannot carry. Dr. Jack Kruse’s public work ranks full-spectrum solar UV at the right time of day over routine capsules and ties skin photoproduction to broader mitochondrial signaling. Those anti-supplement-default claims are his teaching layer—stronger than standard endocrinology’s “sun plus supplement when needed.”

sections.heading: How to use it here

articles.title: Outside Time

sections.heading: Why one activity, three slots

Place sun times route each practice: morning from sunrise until 1.5 hours before solar noon; peak sun for the symmetrical ±1.5-hour window around solar noon (the UVB-centered band); afternoon from then until sunset. Peak sun is where vitamin D synthesis is most efficient per minute when season allows. Morning and afternoon still train outdoor spectrum and movement—just with different UV profiles.

sections.heading: Practical habit
sections.body: Step outside on purpose. Prefer full sun when safe and non-burning; shade still can help at a more limited signal. Build duration gradually. Glass does not count as outside. Pair peak-sun practices with the solar-noon vitamin D lesson when repletion is your goal. Repeat the practice when you go out again in a different slot.

sections.heading: What is solid vs framework
sections.body: Solid ground: outdoor daylight differs from indoor LEDs in intensity and spectrum; solar noon UVB matters for vitamin D; non-burning exposure is the safe pattern. Framework: that every shaded minute is worthless, or that Outside Time replaces sunrise eye light. They are complementary—eyes at dawn, skin and day spectrum through Outside Time.

articles.title: Sun over the horizon

Circadian biology resets from outdoor light intensity and spectrum at the eyes. When the sun itself appears, you get a rapid change in radiance and a solar-path signal indoor LEDs cannot mimic. sections.heading: Why it is the strongest morning signal
sections.body: Glass filters UV and alters spectrum; sunglasses block the dose. Horizon viewing within a tight window around local sunrise is the cleanest natural “day has started” cue. Open-sky and limited-sky outdoor mornings still help—they are lower tiers when weather or terrain block the disk. The hierarchy teaches light quality first, not perfectionism every calendar day.

sections.heading: Practical habit
sections.body: Be outside before the disk clears the horizon when you can. Bare eyes to the sun—no window glass. Bracket local sunrise (shown on Place context) within about 15 minutes before or after for the strongest signal. Pair with outdoor grounding when practical. Practice skin contact and sunglasses on the sunrise practice because they adjust your morning-light response.

sections.heading: What is solid vs framework
sections.body: Solid ground: morning outdoor light is the strongest non-drug circadian zeitgeber; unobstructed outdoor dawn beats indoor brightness. Framework / teaching layer: exact mitochondrial membrane-alignment claims tied to the disk minute. Dr. Jack Kruse’s light-first teaching ranks horizon sunrise at the top of the morning stack; chronobiology agrees on outdoor morning light without requiring a ritual disk every day.

sections.heading: Why open sky still matters
sections.body: Circadian dose depends on outdoor intensity and spectrum at the eyes, not only on seeing a crisp sun disk. A broad sky floods the retina with natural morning light. Glass filters that dose; sunglasses blunt it. Urban canyons and heavy tree cover push you toward the limited-sky tier; a park or rooftop with open sky belongs here.

sections.heading: Practical habit
sections.body: Eyes open to outdoor light without sunglasses when safe. A few minutes can help; longer is fine. Avoid glass between you and the sky when you can. Practice in the sunrise phase when this is your best available signal. Upgrade to horizon viewing on clear days when the disk is visible.

articles.title: Why sunrise is the most important part of the day
articles.summary: Morning outdoor light as the daily reset for circadian clocks, mitochondrial timing, and fat metabolism—what is settled, what is framework, and how to practice it.

sections.heading: Why this comes first
sections.body: If you only change one thing about your day, make it morning outdoor light—ideally around sunrise. Your body does not run on genes as the main “software.” Cells amplify ancient energy pathways that began in light- and energy-rich environments. Clock genes help stabilize biochemistry for the light you actually get; they do not invent metabolism from scratch. Mainstream chronobiology agrees that the solar day–night cycle is the strongest non-drug timer for human circadian clocks. In Dr. Jack Kruse’s light-first teaching (reading Nick Lane’s mitochondrial bioenergetics work), morning solar electromagnetic fields are the daily switch that retunes mitochondrial timing so fat-burning pathways can run cleanly. Whether or not you accept every stronger claim, the practical rule is the same: light before screens, light before food, outdoors when you can.

sections.heading: Living cells vs lab samples
sections.body: A lot of textbook biology comes from tissue that was cut, fixed, homogenized, or fractionated—methods that drain water and freeze a living system into static parts. From that work we get Mitchell’s famous chemiosmotic picture of ATP synthase as the main engine. Kruse’s critique is that those prepared samples under-explain how much energy a living mammal needs in real time. In his light–water–magnetism frame, classical ATP synthase accounts for for only part of the story; sunlight interacting with water and melanin is argued to supply a large share of cellular energy in vivo. That extension draws on earlier bioelectric thinkers such as Gilbert Ling and Robert O. Becker, and it is a teaching layer—not a settled Nobel rewrite. What Lane and Kruse both emphasize, and what is easier to stand on, is simpler: mitochondria are electrical, membrane-organized machines. Timing and environment matter as much as the enzyme list.

sections.heading: What sunrise does to mitochondria
sections.body: Kruse’s Leptin Rx–era teaching puts it this way: the places the TCA cycle (your main fat-and-carb oxidation loop) runs are tied to membranes packed with lipid rafts that convert sunlight into a steady, battery-like charge. That charge helps keep TCA cycling forward so mitochondria burn fat. Miss morning outdoor light and that charge does not set well—fat oxidation feels “expensive,” skin ages faster, and later UV is harder on under-prepared skin. He also talks about inner mitochondrial membrane junctions lining up with the morning solar signal so fat-burning machinery runs in phase. Exact junction-alignment claims and ATP fractions are Kruse-specific. Circadian control of metabolic enzymes is mainstream. Either way, the lifestyle translation is concrete: get eyes (and preferably some skin) into outdoor morning light near sunrise, without glass between you and the sky when you can.

sections.heading: Clocks in the brain, skin, and gut
sections.body: You have a central pacemaker in the brain’s SCN and peripheral clocks in nearly every cell. Special retinal cells—intrinsically photosensitive ganglion cells, or ipRGCs—sense overall brightness and spectrum (researchers often talk about melanopic daylight illuminance as the modern way to estimate circadian dose). Those cells talk to the SCN. CLOCK/BMAL1 loops (with PERs and CRYs) then create roughly 24-hour gene rhythms that gate metabolism, cell repair, and drug responses. Skin clocks help set gut clocks; food can shift some peripheral rhythms, but light and food are not interchangeable. Kruse’s meal line—“eat like a king about half an hour after sunrise, a prince at lunch, a pauper at dinner”—follows from that hierarchy: daylight living disorders molecular clocks; night (melatonin and related repair signals) cleans up; morning sun re-synchronizes the repaired fleet. Phase-response curves in chronobiology quantify how timed light advances or delays the clock; this guide does not measure dim-light melatonin onset in a lab—it teaches the habit that aims at the same biology.

sections.heading: One octave of sun in a noisy spectrum
sections.body: The electromagnetic spectrum is enormous. Visible sunlight is only about one octave of frequency doubling in that vast range. Kruse’s long-standing question is whether artificial light, phones, and network RF drown the organism’s natural “music.” Blue-rich night light delays melatonin; time-varying human-made fields and indoor LEDs add more noise to redox and free-radical signaling inside mitochondria. Genes respond to electromagnetic timing; they do not override a broken light environment. Shift work, sleeping through sunrise, and living under screens all break the same rule: we invented lighting that runs the pathway wrong for almost everyone.

sections.heading: Signals that your morning light habit is missing
sections.body: In Kruse’s teaching—not a diagnostic routine—chronic failure to handle fat well when morning light is missing can show up as dry or scaly skin and poor sleep, dry eyes, feeling cold all the time, dry hair or hair loss, hormonal disruption, low melatonin, constant hunger, mental fog, fat-soluble vitamin issues, stools that never settle, and stubborn weight. Treat those as lifestyle red flags pointing back to sunrise and true dark nights—not as a substitute for medical evaluation.

sections.heading: What is solid, what is framework
sections.body: Solid ground: morning outdoor light is the strongest non-drug circadian zeitgeber; evening blue light delays melatonin; peripheral clocks track the central clock; metabolic pathways are circadian. Credit Lane for pushing membrane bioenergetics and the electric story of mitochondria into public view. Kruse’s disagreements—especially that classical ATP accounting underweights melanin, water, and full-spectrum solar EMF—are his teaching layer. This guide presents his practical hierarchy pedagogically: horizon-disk sunrise over open sky over “just outside,” no glass when possible, light before food—not as lab dosimetry.

sections.heading: How to use it here
sections.body: Practice sunrise light (horizon, open sky, or outside) before screens. Better outdoor signals support a stronger morning signal—teaching light first, then everything else. Pair with sunset viewing, evening blue-light hygiene, and true dark sleep so overnight repair can happen before the next sunrise re-synchronizes the fleet. Outside Time near solar noon is a separate skin/UV habit, not a substitute for morning eye light. Educational only—not medical advice. articles.title: Why watching the sunset matters
articles.summary: Evening outdoor light as the circadian wind-down: warmer spectrum, melatonin timing, and the Light habit of bare-eye sunset before true dark.

sections.heading: What sunset viewing is
sections.body: Sunset viewing means being outdoors as the sun goes down—patio, yard, walk, or west-facing view—with bare eyes when glare allows. Morning outdoor light advances the day clock; sunset closes the outdoor arc before true dark. You do not need a perfect horizon disk the way the sunrise keystone tiers work. Being outside while the sky dims is the habit This guide covers.

sections.heading: Why it matters for circadian timing
sections.body: As the sun lowers, the spectrum shifts toward longer wavelengths—more red and near-infrared relative to blue—and intensity falls. Melanopsin-rich retinal cells are less driven by that warm, lower light than by noon blue sky, which is part of why evening outdoor viewing feels calmer than a laptop screen. Chronobiology research emphasizes structure: bright day, dim warm evening, dark night. Sunset is the last natural outdoor photon dose, signaling “day is ending” to clocks that never read wall-clock time.

sections.heading: Melatonin, screens, and the handoff indoors
sections.body: Melatonin onset is delayed by evening blue-enriched artificial light. Watching the actual sun go down outdoors gives a natural, lower-blue signal before you move inside. The useful stack is sunset outdoors first, then dim warm bulbs and warmer screens—not jumping from bright kitchen LEDs straight into bed. Skipping sunset and living under cool LEDs all evening fights the gradient your body expects.

sections.heading: Practical habit
sections.body: Be outside 10–20 minutes bracketing local sunset when weather allows. Bare eyes; skip sunglasses in that window unless glare forces them. Afterward, dim indoor lighting rather than snapping back to bright LEDs. Cloudy days still count: open-sky dimming trains timing even without a visible solar disk. Reminders can use “30 min before sunset” or “At sunset” from your ZIP sun times.

sections.heading: What is solid vs framework
sections.body: Solid ground: evening blue-rich light can delay melatonin; dim, warm evenings and dark nights support sleep timing; outdoor light at dusk is a natural wind-down cue. Framework / teaching layer: mandatory horizon-disk sunset rituals, exact minute prescriptions, and stronger UV-A exhaustion claims at sunset as mitochondrial rules. Dr. Jack Kruse’s public material treats sunset as the bookend to sunrise—outdoor natural light at both transitions, then blocking artificial blue after the solar signal ends. Mainstream sleep medicine agrees on dim evenings without requiring a ritual disk sighting.

sections.heading: What true dark means
sections.body: True dark is not “I closed my eyes.” It means the room stays dark if you open them: no street glow through curtains, no TV standby LEDs, no charger indicators, no bright clock faces. Practical tools: blackout curtains or shades, tape or covers on status LEDs, phone in another room or far from the bed on airplane mode, and an eye mask when travel or partners make perfect blackout impossible.

sections.heading: Why darkness is half the light story
sections.body: The Light pillar is not only sunrise and outdoor day spectrum—it is also denying wrong light at night. Circadian biology trains on contrast: bright, blue-rich outdoor day versus dim, warm evening versus true dark during sleep. When street glow or a phone screen keeps melanopsin-active signals after sunset, melatonin suppression and sleep fragmentation follow in controlled studies. Sleep medicine ranks a dark bedroom with morning light and stable timing as baseline hygiene. Here darkness is under Light because you are managing photons.

sections.heading: Melatonin, sleep depth, and night glow
sections.body: Melatonin rises in dim evening light and is blunted by blue-enriched screens or bright room light. Light leaks can lighten sleep and shrink deep-stage time in some lab work. Pair bedroom darkness with evening blue-light hygiene so you are not fighting an hour of bright phone before you expect pitch black. Standby LEDs inches from the face count as light pollution; routers and TVs add RF noise too. Phone away from bed is both a light and field habit.

sections.heading: Practical habit
sections.body: Walk the room once with lights off and eyes open. Cover every emitter you can see. Prefer blackout over “pretty sheer.” Keep chargers and glowing clocks out of the sight line of the pillow. When you travel, pack an eye mask. Cool room temperature and a consistent sleep window amplify the same night recovery story—darkness alone is not the whole stack.

sections.body: Solid ground: dark sleep supports melatonin timing; even low bedroom light can matter for sensitive people; morning outdoor light plus night dark is the core contrast. Framework / teaching layer: that every LED is actively harmful nnEMF-adjacent stress that wrecks mitochondrial recovery unless removed. Dr. Jack Kruse stresses true darkness—not dim—plus removing phones and routers from the sleep space in his night stack. Mainstream chronobiology already agrees on dark sleep; his coupling to redox and nnEMF is the stronger teaching layer.
